extracted.intended_audience: general readers; readers of 19th-century voyage narratives, naturalists, and colonial administrators
extracted.subtask_description: A 19th-century shipboard travel narrative describing islands, peoples, natural productions, anchorage surveys, trade, and settlement prospects from a voyaging naturalist/observer's perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nutmeg curing/process for export
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps and timing for processing nutmegs from harvest to export.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harvest about nine months after blossom; gather fruit resembling an unripe peach with a tough fleshy skin that splits in two. Separate the mace (partly enveloping the nut) and dry it for two or three days in the sun. Place nutmegs on long bamboo platforms under sheds and dry by means of wood fires. When sufficiently dry, hand over to Government stores (in this context) where they are heated with quick-lime to preserve them from insects; then ready for export.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchorage suitability criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Features used to judge whether a harbour or anchorage is convenient and safe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider water depth for convenient anchorage (too deep is unsuitable); whether harbour is sheltered in prevailing monsoons; width and safety of passages (narrow but safe channels can be used by keeping a particular shore); presence of shoals and their effect on approach; availability of anchorage in different monsoon wind directions (some anchorages good in one monsoon but exposed in the opposite).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timber export potential indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: How to assess whether island timber could become a valuable export.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for varieties highly prized for durability and ease of working; trees of immense size that are almost invariably sound; proximity of timber to the beach so they can be felled and brought out easily—these factors make timber promising as an export commodity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing local trade markets and preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations to determine what manufactured goods will sell in different island markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that less civilized parts of the archipelago prefer cheap goods and gaudy patterns (British cotton manufactures sell there), while people of more settled islands (e.g., Java, Celebes) prefer their own or Indian manufactures which are dearer but more durable. Use such tastes to choose export goods for trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimating voyage profitability and trade volume
rubrics_metrics.description: How to estimate returns from local trading proas and annual import/export value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reported imports per vessel (e.g., each Bughis proa imports 10,000–30,000 dollars) and cargo profit ratios (a return cargo value around 200% on outlay) combined with fleet counts to estimate annual trade volumes and values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surveying and chart-validation practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles for coastal surveying and the need to re-examine poorly charted groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When charts are inaccurate, conduct detailed examination to discover anchoring-places and safe approaches; a rough survey can suggest many more safe anchorages than indicated on faulty charts. Keep in mind that mischarted islands/groups require more time for examination than a cursory visit allows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of missionary establishment 'success'
rubrics_metrics.description: What counts as evidence that missionary work has taken root in a native village.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of a church and schoolhouse built under missionary direction, school attendance by native children, and observable conversion (e.g., natives described as converted). Also note that social stressors (drought, famine) can quickly undermine missionary influence if old beliefs are reasserted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing settlement prospects and commercial value
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors to consider when judging the future importance of a remote settlement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the site's harbor quality (good anchorages, shelter), proximity to trade routes and islands rich in products, potential for steam/coaling depots (strategic position), unexplored hinterland resources, and capacity to serve as an emporium linking archipelago products with continental produce. Avoid relying solely on immediate local fertility; consider wider regional trade potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health and climate assessment for European settlers
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria affecting the salubrity of a settlement and suitability for Europeans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider housing adequacy (small, low thatched cottages in hot climates may encourage disease), nearby mangrove swamps that may reduce salubrity, thermometer ranges (examples: as low as 62°F, average about 83°F in the text), exposure to heat causing conditions like coup de soleil, and recorded local morbidity/mortality. Local meteorological records and medical journals are useful supplements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating native social/economic conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Observational signs used to appraise native welfare and causes of poverty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for evidence of poverty despite rich produce (e.g., widespread use of spirituous liquors brought by traders), cultivated but exhausted soils, abandoned farms, and effects of drought/famine on food supply. Such signs help explain social conditions and the limits to local prosperity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small-boat trading safety considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational risks and advice when conducting trade with natives from larger vessels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where anchorages are poor and boats must be sent in to trade, crews are divided and more vulnerable to treachery; locating anchorages where vessels can come close in and trade directly reduces risk. Use caution trading at poorly sheltered coasts or with tribes warned as untrustworthy (the page names Timor Laut and Baba as such).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nutmeg and clove quality/market differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: How to judge which local spice produce will find European/Chinese markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess pearls and spices by form and hue (e.g., irregular, golden-hued pearls prized by Chinese but not Europeans; smaller, more perfect pearls have broader appeal). Compare local clove quality against known standards (Amboyna cloves prized more than Banda's), as only higher-quality produce will fetch export value.
